meta.title: Who really said "I Have the Simplest Tastes; I Am Always Satisfied with the Best"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Wilde probably did say it — but the only source is Edgar Saltus's 1917 memoir, printed 17 years after Wilde died. And Churchill never said his version.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I Have the Simplest Tastes; I Am Always Satisfied with the Best'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to page 20 of Edgar Saltus's 1917 memoir of Wilde — a friend's posthumous recollection, not Wilde's own writing. The Churchill version is Lord Birkenhead's.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Wilde — and unusually for a Wilde quip, it does sit in a dated, checkable book. But it is not a book Wilde wrote. The words are Edgar Saltus’s recollection of a conversation, printed on page 20 of Oscar Wilde: An Idler’s Impression (Chicago, 1917), seventeen years after Wilde died. Nothing in Wilde’s own hand carries the line, so the credit rests on one friend’s memory.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Edgar Saltus, recalling Wilde in conversation
Brothers of the Book, Chicago, 1917 — first edition of 474 copies

source.excerpt:
I put a bold face on it. “Come to my shop,” I said, “and have dinner with me. Though,” I added, “I don’t know what I can give you.”

“Oh, anything,” Wilde replied. “Anything, no matter what. I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best.”

He was not boasting. One evening he dined on his “Sphinx.” Subsequently I supped with him on “Salome.”
trail: The scene, undated — Saltus arrives a week late for dinner at Wilde’s London house, apologises by inviting Wilde to eat with him instead, and admits he may have little to offer. Wilde’s reply is the quote. Saltus records no year for the evening. The passage on Wikisource ↗
30 November 1900 — Wilde dies in Paris, aged 46. Everything that follows is posthumous. Wikipedia ↗

1917 — Saltus publishes Oscar Wilde: An Idler’s Impression with Brothers of the Book of Chicago, in a first edition of 474 copies, the type distributed and no second edition planned. The quip is on page 20. Project Gutenberg ↗

2012 — Quote Investigator reviews the case, points to the same 1917 page, judges the evidence for Wilde strong while flagging the posthumous printing, and finds no evidence Winston Churchill ever said the version bearing his name. Quote Investigator ↗
source.excerptNote: Saltus prints the quip as two sentences separated by a full stop. The semicolon form now in wide circulation is a later smoothing, not the punctuation on the page. Saltus gives no date for the evening.

source.rightsNote: The work carrying this line — Edgar Saltus, Oscar Wilde: An Idler’s Impression — was first published in Chicago in 1917, well before the 1931 US copyright cutoff, and is therefore in the public domain in the United States. Both Project Gutenberg and Wikisource host the complete text on that basis. Wilde’s own words, spoken before his death in 1900, carry no separate live claim.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.kicker: The man the line is pinned on
author.heading: Who was Oscar Wilde?
author.bio: Oscar Fingal O’Fflahertie Wills Wilde was an Irish author, poet and playwright, born in Dublin on 16 October 1854 and dead in Paris on 30 November 1900. He was a central figure in the Aestheticism movement and, by the early 1890s, one of the most popular dramatists in London — Lady Windermere’s Fan, An Ideal Husband, The Importance of Being Earnest — before his 1895 conviction for gross indecency ended his career. His reputation as a talker is precisely the problem for quote-hunters: the epigrams that made him famous were often spoken, and survive only because someone else wrote them down later.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Two things go wrong with this line. It gets reassigned to a different famous wit, and the wording gets smoothed out. Neither the Churchill version nor the tidy semicolon version matches what is actually on the page.

items.why: “I am a man of simple tastes; I am easily satisfied with the best” is one of the most-circulated Churchill lines online. Quote Investigator found no evidence Churchill ever said it of himself. The remark was reportedly made about him by F. E. Smith, Lord Birkenhead — as Randolph Churchill told the columnist Leonard Lyons in a 1948 newspaper piece: “Mr. Churchill is a man of very simple tastes. He is always prepared to put up with the best of everything.” Quote Investigator ↗

The 1917 page prints two separate sentences divided by a full stop. The semicolon form used as this page’s headline, and the smoother variant “I’m a man of simple tastes. I’m always satisfied with the best,” both circulate under Wilde’s name; neither is the punctuation or phrasing Saltus set in type. Compare the 1917 text ↗

Even the Wilde credit is one man’s memory of a conversation, written down long afterwards and published in a 474-copy private edition. That is why Wikiquote lists the line under Attributed rather than among Wilde’s sourced works. Wikiquote ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The best-documented version is the one on page 20 of Saltus’s memoir. Offered dinner at short notice and warned there might not be much of it, Wilde answers: “Oh, anything. Anything, no matter what. I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best.” Read the passage ↗

context.heading: Why this one is better documented than most Wilde quips
lead: Most of the epigrams pinned on Wilde have no paper trail at all. This one does. Edgar Saltus was an American novelist of the decadent school whose work ran parallel to Wilde’s, and who knew him personally — his memoir opens with their first meeting at Delmonico’s in New York, and moves on to Wilde married, bourgeois and domestic in his London house. The exchange in question is small and domestic too: Saltus turns up a week late for dinner, tries to cover the embarrassment by inviting Wilde out instead, and warns him there may not be much to eat.

The reply is the quote. What makes it feel authentic is the sentence Saltus puts immediately after it — a flat, unshowy aside that reads like a man remembering rather than a man inventing an epigram. But the memoir appeared in 1917, in an edition of 474 copies, seventeen years after Wilde was buried. Nobody can now check it against Wilde. That gap is the whole reason this page says “attributed” and not “verified.”
context.detailsSummary: How the line drifted onto Winston Churchill
detailsBody: The joke has a second life under Churchill’s name, usually as “I am a man of simple tastes; I am easily satisfied with the best.” Quote Investigator found no evidence Churchill said any such thing about himself. What it did find was the remark being made about him: Randolph Churchill, quoted by the columnist Leonard Lyons in 1948, credited it to F. E. Smith, Lord Birkenhead.

A jest that flatters the speaker is much funnier when a friend says it about you than when you say it about yourself — which is roughly the difference between the Birkenhead version and the internet’s Churchill version. Quote Investigator notes it is possible Smith was working, directly or indirectly, from Wilde’s earlier line.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator traces "I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best" to Edgar Saltus's 1917 book Oscar Wilde: An Idler's Impression, quote page 20 (Brothers of the Book, Chicago); concludes there is strong evidence Wilde made the remark though it was printed posthumously; finds no evidence Winston Churchill said the similar line himself, and reports that Randolph Churchill, quoted by Leonard Lyons in the Greensboro Record of 28 July 1948, credited it to Lord Birkenhead saying of his father: "Mr. Churchill is a man of very simple tastes. He is always prepared to put up with the best of everything."

Wikisource's transcription of Saltus's Oscar Wilde, an Idler's Impression (1917) contains the exchange verbatim: Saltus offers dinner, and Wilde replies "Oh, anything ... Anything, no matter what. I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best." followed by "He was not boasting." The header records the work as by Edgar Saltus, 1917.

Project Gutenberg eBook #32849 is the full text of Oscar Wilde: An Idler's Impression by Edgar Saltus; its title page reads "CHICAGO / BROTHERS OF THE BOOK / 1917" with "Copyright 1917 by Edgar Saltus", its colophon states 474 copies were printed with the type distributed and no second edition to be made, and the body contains the exact wording "I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best."

The Internet Archive holds a scan of the 1917 edition of Oscar Wilde, an idler's impression by Edgar Saltus; its full text contains the quote, and the printed page number [20] appears immediately after the passage, confirming the page-20 citation.

Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde article lists "I have the simplest tastes. I am always satisfied with the best." under its Attributed section, sourced as "Reported in Edgar Saltus, Oscar Wilde: An Idler's Impression (1917), p. 20" — not in a sourced-works section.

Wikipedia records Oscar Wilde as an Irish author, poet and playwright, born 16 October 1854 in Dublin and died 30 November 1900 in Paris, a key figure in Aestheticism and among the most popular London dramatists of the early 1890s, convicted in 1895 of gross indecency.
Wikipedia describes Edgar Evertson Saltus as an American writer of highly refined prose whose works paralleled those of European decadent authors including Oscar Wilde.
